column5: Population vs sample (and why we sample). Non-probability methods (convenience/accidental, quota, purposive, snowball, consecutive) vs probability methods (simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster): one everyday example each, plus a "how to tell them apart" table (stratified vs cluster and quota vs stratified are classic MCQ traps). Parameter (μ, σ², p) vs statistic (x̄, S², p̂) table. EX 5.1–5.3. Pure-concept MCQ material, so include at least 8 MCQ practice items.

Idea: x̄ changes from sample to sample, so it has its own distribution with mean μ and SD σ/√n (standard error). Why a bigger n gives a narrower curve. Central Limit Theorem (n≥30). Z=(x̄−μ)/(σ/√n). Cases: normal and σ known; σ unknown with n≥30 (use S); non-normal with n≥30. EX 5.4, EX 5.5 (p-29 height), EX 5.8. Side-by-side comparison with lesson 07: "one X" vs "the average of n".

When we must use t (normal population, σ unknown, n<30). Shape vs Z (fatter tails, becomes Z as df grows). Degrees of freedom ν=n−1. T=(x̄−μ)/(S/√n). HOW TO READ THE t TABLE (row ν, column = right-tail area; flag ⚠️ the header that says Cum.prob). Finding t₀ for a given probability, negative t by symmetry. EX 5.5 (p-32 table exercise — explain the duplicate EX number), EX 5.6, EX 5.7. A decision box: Z or t?
Sample proportion p̂ = x/n, its mean p and SD √(p(1−p)/n), Z for p̂, large-sample condition. Link back to binomial (lesson 04). EX 5.9, EX 5.10. Flag ⚠️ p-38 μ_p̂ printed as μ (should be p).

Two independent groups: x̄₁−x̄₂ has mean μ₁−μ₂. Three cases with one decision table: (1) σ₁, σ₂ known or both n≥30 gives Z; (2) small samples with equal variances gives pooled t, Sp², df n₁+n₂−2; (3) small samples with unequal variances gives Welch t with the Welch df formula (show the calculator steps slowly, and how to round df for the table). EX 5.11–5.15 (EX 5.11 is the Z case with known σ). Flag the EX 5.12 n=25 condition issue.

p̂₁−p̂₂: mean p₁−p₂, SD formula, Z. EX 5.16 (explain "แตกต่างน้อยกว่า 8%" as an absolute difference and show the interpretation the slide intends). Finish with a one-page CH5 summary table: statistic → mean → SD → Z or t → condition.

Why estimate; point estimate (x̄ for μ, p̂ for p, S² for σ²) vs interval estimate; what "95% confidence" really means (not "95% chance μ is inside this one interval" — explain simply); α = 1 − confidence; Z_{α/2} values 90%/95%/99% = 1.645/1.96/2.575 (show how to get them from the exam Z table; note 2.575 vs 2.58 rounding); general shape estimate ± (critical value × standard error); width vs confidence vs n. EX 6.1, 6.2.

CI for μ, three cases (σ known: Z; σ unknown with n≥30: Z with S; normal, σ unknown, n<30: t with ν=n−1). Flag ⚠️ the p-12 heading vs theorem mismatch. EX 6.3, 6.4, 6.5 with full calculator steps. A "which case?" mini-flowchart.
CI for p: p̂ ± Z_{α/2}√(p̂q̂/n). EX 6.6. Common slips (using a percentage instead of a decimal, forgetting the square root, using n−1).

CI for μ₁−μ₂: Z case (known σ or large n), pooled t (equal variances, Sp², ν=n₁+n₂−2), Welch t (unequal variances, Welch ν). Keep the group order; a negative interval and an interval containing 0 mean something — explain. EX 6.7, 6.8, 6.9 (EX 6.9 has raw data: compute x̄ and S step by step with the calculator).

column5: Paired data (same person before/after): build Dᵢ, D̄, S_D, CI with t ν=n−1; how to recognise paired vs independent from the wording. CI for p₁−p₂. EX 6.10, 6.11. End with a CH6 summary table of all 6 CI formulas plus "use when".

Courtroom analogy (H₀ = innocent until proven guilty). H₀ always contains =; H₁ comes from the claim words (มากกว่า >, น้อยกว่า <, เปลี่ยนแปลง/แตกต่าง ≠) with a big word-to-symbol table. Type I error (α) and Type II error (β), power 1−β, with the 2x2 decision table. One-tailed vs two-tailed, critical value, rejection region (draw in words / ASCII). The 5 steps of a test (slide p-18). The p-value idea in plain language. "Reject H₀" vs "do not reject H₀" (never "accept/prove H₀" — but the slides say ยอมรับ H₀: explain both wordings). EX 7.1 (flag ⚠️ the p-05 μ≠60 error), EX 7.2. Note there is no EX 7.3 in the slides.

Test for μ: Z (σ known), Z with S (n≥30), t (normal, n<30, σ unknown). Every example uses the 5 steps, both the critical-value method and the p-value method. EX 7.4, 7.5, 7.6, 7.7. Where the slide gives no α, write "สมมติ α = 0.05" and also say what changes at α = 0.01.
Test for p: Z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀q₀/n) — use p₀ (not p̂) in the SD and explain why. EX 7.8, 7.9 (EX 7.9 "อย่างน้อย 90%" claim: which side is H₁).
Test for μ₁−μ₂ with d₀: Z case, pooled t, Welch t (reuse the decision table from lesson 14). EX 7.10, 7.11, 7.12. Don't forget d₀ when it isn't 0.
Paired test: Dᵢ, D̄, S_D, T with ν=n−1 (Z if n large). Choosing the direction of D (before − after) and how it flips the sign of H₁. EX 7.13, 7.14.

Test for p₁−p₂: pooled p̂ when d₀=0, separate SE when d₀≠0. EX 7.15 (flag the "มากกว่าอยู่ร้อยละ 1" ambiguity), EX 7.16. End with a CH7 summary table of all tests: hypothesis → statistic → table → df.
